newsitem.title: FRANCE: French trial will target Papon Resistance claim.
newsitem.headline: French trial will target Papon Resistance claim.

text.p: Relatives of French wartime deportees preparing for the trial of accused Nazi collaborator Maurice Papon have launched a determined campaign to discredit his insistence he was a member of the Resistance.
Capping 15 years of legal manoeuvres, Papon, 86, is expected to go before a jury this autumn on charges he sent 1,560 Jews, many of them children, to Nazi death camps.

The trial, which could last three to four months, is expected to focus on a dark chapter in French history when many supporters of the occupiers' Vichy government, sensing a shift in the tide of the war, quietly changed sides themselves.
In a preview of his defence, the former secretary-general of the Bordeaux prefect's office during 1942-44 argued -- among other things -- that he had been active in the Resistance.

"I disobeyed all the time, I served the Resistance, I carried out sabotage," Papon said in a rare television interview on Tuesday, insisting he had kept his post in the Vichy administration at the request of his underground leaders.

But lawyer Gerard Boulanger, who will represent deportees' relatives at the trial, said: "We are going to fight from now on to clear up Mr Papon's false Resistance documentation and the scandal that he still wears his Legion of Honour ribbon".
Before the discovery of dusty wartime files documenting his arrests and deportation orders, Papon had been named commander of the Legion of Honour, France's highest honour.
Before his wartime record became known, Papon enjoyed a meteoric post-war career, serving as Paris police chief in the 1960s and then as budget minister in the 1970s.

When the incriminating documents were first disclosed in May 1981, Papon claimed he was being set up by leftists. He called for a jury of honour made up of five former Resistance members to judge the evidence.

The jury's conclusion, rendered in December 1981 was ambiguous, saying that Papon "contributed to certain acts that did not conform with the jury's concept of honour" and should have resigned from his official duties in 1942.
But it added that he did try to help certain Jews and concluded charges against him were unjustified.
Nonetheless, Papon was later indicted in January 1983 on charges of "crimes against humanity".
For Leon Boutbien, president of the Union of Deportees and Resistance Members, Papon's credentials are impeccable.

"His participation in the Resistance is absolutely confirmed," Boutbien told Reuters. "The most prestigious of personalities have borne witness to this. Would someone have been decorated, without an investigation, had he committed nearly 1,600 crimes?"

But a French court which examined the evidence in the case to determine whether Papon should stand trial, concluded there was no proof he was in the Resistance though he had certainly done favours for Resistance leaders.
Lawyers for the deportees' relatives told Reuters they believe Papon tried to "whitewash" his past in 1958, when he was named Paris police chief.

"Despite numerous research efforts, we have never found a trace of Resistance activity on the part of Maurice Papon in the Gironde department," said Andre Dartigues, president of the Bordeaux Committee for the History of the Resistance.
